speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 5, to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill No. 5 proposes three amendments to the Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935. The first amendment corrects an error in section 20. In this section reference is made to the "thirty-first day of August". The amendment corrects this date to the "first day of August", as was intended.
The other two amendments are proposed as a result of experience in the operation of the Canadian wheat board over the years.
Under the act as it now stands, any increase in the initial payment for wheat, oats, and barley made during a pool period or crop year must be equal for all grades. A situation could arise in which it might be possible to increase the initial payment for certain grades of wheat, oats or barley to a greater extent than for other grades of the same grain. This amendment is designed to give the governor in council some latitude in adjusting initial payments within the crop year as between grades. I do not anticipate that the powers asked for in this amendment would be used in a year of normal production. On the other hand, I believe that the amendment, if enacted, will be useful in the event of a crop in which there are not only wide variations among the grades, but wide variations in the demand for particular grades as well. The proposed amendment is intended to meet such a contingency, rather than to alter procedures followed in a normal crop year.
The third amendment is the most important of the three. It proposes a means by which annual pools may be wound up promptly. Occasions have arisen in the past when the board has been operating two or more pool accounts at the same time. The procedure in these cases has been to divide sales between the pools. This means that the winding up of a particular pool takes an

Canadian Wheat Board Act unreasonable length of time. The amendment gives the governor in council power to authorize the transfer of unsold grain from one pool account to the next pool account for the purpose of winding up the earlier account and permitting a final payment as soon as possible after the end of each crop year.
The amendment contemplates a careful valuation of the inventory to be transferred, with the principle in mind that the later pool should neither gain nor lose because of the unsold grain transferred to it. In actual practice it may not be possible to eliminate all risk to the pools concerned. I believe that the house will agree, however, that the proposed method is preferable to holding up the final settlement with producers under each pool until such time as the last of the grain in that pool has been sold.
I have now covered all the matters concerning Bill No. 5, but I am sure the hon. members would wish me to take this occasion to review the current developments in the board's operations.
I shall not discuss the 1945-49 pool account at this time, as it will be the subject of special legislation to be brought down shortly. I might say just this, however, for the information of hon. members, that the annual report of the board has now been completed in Winnipeg and has been laid on the table of the house at an earlier sitting. The report contains the accounts covering the 1945-49 pool wheat, the last of which wheat was disposed of in December, 1950.
We are going through a most unusual experience in the marketing of wheat this year. The unusual circumstances arise largely from the lateness of the 1950 harvest and from the extensive damage to quality sustained by nearly one-half the crop due to the frosts last August.
The lateness of the 1950 harvest reduced the volume of shipments from country elevators to the lakehead before the close of navigation and made the transportation of grain an acute and continuing problem for the remainder of the crop year 1950-51. Because of the late harvest, some 37,000 fewer cars of grain were loaded in the prairie provinces from August 1 to December 1, 1950, than were loaded the corresponding period a year ago, despite the fact that the railways loaded cars in the country at about the same rate as last year once the 1950 crop started to move. In recent weeks the loadings have been exceeding last year's levels.
In marketing the 1950 wheat crop, the Canadian wheat board is carrying on two distinct operations, the one having to do with milling wheat, the other with the lower grades. As a result of the frost damage and

unfavourable harvesting weather, less than one-third of the 1950 crop will fall into the grades Nos. 1, 2 and 3 northern, which are the standard milling grades normally constituting the bulk of the prairie wheat crop. Fortunately we had a carry-over of about 99 million bushels of wheat on July 31 last, principally of the grade No. 2 northern. In addition, No. 4 northern wheat this year has been a useful milling grade both in the domestic market and for export. Even allowing for these factors, our supplies of milling grades of wheat are not adequate to meet the demand this year. In selling the milling grades, the board's problem is one of securing adequate transportation both by rail and by inland water routes to meet domestic and export commitments.
I might add that Alberta marketings of wheat show a high percentage of milling grades, and as a result the board is working on a maximum export program through Pacific coast ports, which will continue for the balance of the crop year.
With respect to low-grade wheat, the situation is very different. Because of the damage sustained in 1950, the board is faced with the task of shipping and selling over 150 million bushels of grades not normally used for milling purposes. Fortunately, the largest individual grade among the lower grades is No. 5 wheat, for which there has been an overseas demand. No. 6 wheat and feed wheat are being sold in some volume to the United States where such wheat can enter on the -basis of a five per cent ad valorem duty, provided that the sample is considered unfit for human consumption. The disposal of such a large quantity of low-grade wheat will take considerably more time than that required for the selling of the limited supplies of milling grades, but progress is being made.
I should also note a third circumstance. As a result of the wet harvesting weather a considerable quantity of grain had an unusually high moisture content on delivery to country elevators and is grading tough and damp. The existence of so much grain with a high moisture content has had the effect of reducing the effective capacity of country elevators and lakehead terminals. I hope it will be possible to find storage for stocks of tough and damp grain remaining on farms, as well as terminal accommodation for the tough and damp stocks still in country elevators, before warm weather sets in. The wheat board and the board of grain commissioners are co-operating to that end. I might add that damp grain has been given first preference in transportation throughout the crop year, and the shipment of tough

Canadian Wheat Board Act
grain of the lower grades has only been limited by the essential requirements of the board for milling grades which include the toughs of these grades.
From October 1 to date about 36,000 cars of tough and damp grain have been inspected. These inspections represent about 33 per cent of total cars inspected during the period. Thus, the shipment of tough and damp grain has received a substantial percentage of cars available for country loadings. Late in January, because of congestion at the lakehead, the board issued instructions limiting shipments of grain to the lakehead to damp grain. Recently it has been possible to amend this restriction to allow high-moisture tough grades to be moved as well.
Terminal elevators at the lakehead have had a free hand in drying damp grain and are keeping abreast with arrivals. Tough grain is being dried as required by the board. Although some 65 million bushels of tough and damp grain have been inspected, it is difficult to estimate the amount still to be shipped. While the problem is undoubtedly a diminishing one, it will continue for some time yet.
Under all these circumstances the Canadian wheat board has endeavoured to follow a balanced shipping policy. It has endeavoured to move forward sufficient high-grade wheat, including toughs and damps of these grades, to take care of moderate export commitments. This has left considerable latitude for the shipment of low-grade grain including the toughs and damps of these grades. The board felt, and I think for good reason, that in spite of the special problems arising from the large volume of low-grade wheat produced in the west this year, and from the volume of tough and damp grain, that a reasonable effort should be made to get on with the marketing of that half of the crop consisting of milling grades.
The board has made good progress in disposing of milling grades of wheat arising from the carry-over from the 1949 crop and from the 1950 crop. Commitments have been made rot only for stocks which have arrived in selling positions, but for stocks which will be shipped from country elevators during the balance of the crop year.
For transportation reasons, sales of wheat of lower grades are not so far advanced, but sufficient sales had been made to give the board confidence in its selling prices for No. 5, No. 6 and feed wheat. By the end of last December it was apparent that wheat of milling grades would be sold at the international wheat agreement maximum price.
With this situation in mind, the board and the government considered it practicable to
increase the initial payment on all grades of wheat by 20 cents per bushel. As hon. members are aware, this increase became effective on February 1. Between August 1, 1950, and January 31, 1951, producers had marketed about 256 million bushels of wheat, upon which an adjustment payment of 20 cents per bushel is about to be made. If the 1950-51 wheat account shows a surplus when all wheat is sold, there will be a final payment to producers. Because of existing good export demand there is reason to believe that there will be a final payment on all grades.
Earlier in the crop year the board felt that it would take perhaps twenty-four months to transport and sell the large volume of low-grade wheat harvested this year. Without minimizing the difficulties ahead in transporting and selling such a large volume of low-grade wheat, the board is now more optimistic.
The movement of oats and barley, for the reasons I have outlined, has been somewhat slower than in the previous crop year but, as in the case of wheat, the board had made good progress in selling both grains by the end of December. In January 1951, the board recommended, and the government approved, an increase in the initial payment on oats of 10 cents per bushel and an increase in the initial payment on barley of 20 cents per bushel, both increases becoming effective on February 1, 1951. Up to the end of January producers had marketed about 59 million bushels of oats and 58 million bushels of barley, against which adjustment payments of 10 cents per bushel and 20 cents per bushel respectively are about to be made. Any surplus in the 1950-51 oats and barley pools at the close of operations will, of course, be paid to producers in final payments.

speechtext:
An amendment to the Canadian Wheat Board Act of 1935 was passed during 1947 providing for the five-year wheat pool, 1945 to 1950. It was retroactive legislation. Members of this party proposed an amendment to the legislation creating the five-year pool, and we were voted down at that time by the supporters of the government. The U.K.-Canada contract went into effect on August 1, 1946. Farmers were compelled to sell 160 million bushels of wheat to the United Kingdom in each of the crop years 1946-47 and 1947-48 at $1.55 a bushel. The price for 140 million bushels in each of the two following years


was to be fixed by negotiation under clause 2(b). The price for 1948-49 and 1949-50 crops was fixed at $2 which recovered none of the loss on the first two years of the contract. In fact the price was much over $2 when that price was negotiated and .greed upon.
On the most conservative estimate the farmers of western Canada lost $330 million in the first two years of the contract. In fact I can break that down into separate years. If anybody cares to check the report made by the then minister of trade and commerce, to be found at page 6020 of Hansard for July 17, 1947, the loss estimated by him was 77 cents per bushel or a total of $123,200,000 on the first year. On the same basis there was a loss of $207 million for the second year making in round figures a total for those two years of just over $330 million. I think these figures should be compared with a portion of the statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in this house on March 2, to be found at page 833 of Hansard. He was announcing -the final settlement of the five-year pool, and at that time he said:
The contribution ... is the equivalent of about 23 cents per bushel on the deliveries made during the last two years of the agreement to which article 2(b) had reference, that Is, the $65 million contribution.
You will see that his statement completely ignored the first two years of the contract. At the time he made the statement it was very confusing to me. It has certainly been confusing to certain provincial ministers of agriculture judging from reports I have read of what they have had to say in their legislatures. Why the Prime Minister worded his statement that way I do not know. It is very interesting to study clause 2 (b) carefully, what actually happened in the first two years, and the Prime Minister's statement.
On the entire contract the loss is estimated at close to $500 million. Because of this wheat agreement the domestic price of wheat in Canada was held down to the level of the agreement. After September, 1946, when other producers and wage earners were freed of controls and able to charge all that the market would bear, the wheat farmers were lashed to an improvident agreement which compelled them to subsidize every bread consumer in Canada. In my opinion there was no shadow of justice in this policy. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) discussed the United Kingdom-Canada wheat agreement on August 14, 1946. I do not think I need to remind the house that he was the minister who a month previously had negotiated the agreement on behalf of the government generally and on behalf of the then

minister of trade and commerce. As appears at page 4810 of Hansard of August 14, 1946, he said:
When we are at the end of the four-year period, if in the last six or twelve months we find ourselves in the position that world markets, so-called, are not offering as much for wheat as we are getting for it, I hope people will stand behind us to the extent they are standing behind us now. Even if wheat stays above $1.55 during the whole period, I hope people will still feel that it was worth while trying. If we are successful in this experiment, then we can talk to the grain trade people with some assurance. If they are able to show us at the end of the five-year period that we were all wrong, that over that length of time the farmer got less than he ever got before under similar circumstances and that the other system would have brought him more, then we shall be in a position to discuss the matter with them on an even footing. I am sure anyone who has taken this position and finds himself wrong will be quite prepared to discuss it from that point of view. In the meantime we are convinced that this is the best thing for the farmer. As long as we are convinced of that, and having another four years in which to try it out, we can put the policy into effect in a way that will at least help us to determine how this long argument between farmer and grain trade in western Canada ought to be settled in the interests of the great masses of the people.

I do not need much help, but I accept it thankfully. The statement

Canadian Wheat Board Act which was then made was to the effect that we were starting on an experiment, and no one had any right to consider it anything other than an experiment. We were hopeful that that experiment would give us some guidance in dealing with a question which had been discussed over a long period of years in western Canada, and in this house as well. I recall that the constituency which I now represent in this house was represented in 1896 by a gentleman, Dr. Douglas, who introduced the first Manitoba Grain Act into this house. He was here as a patron of industry, the name under which the farm movement of his day operated; and he brought into this house a bill, a private member's bill, which he thought should be passed by the house, to deal with the marketing of wheat on the Winnipeg grain exchange. He had the same experience as private members have here at the present time, Mr. Speaker. He had his bill talked out the first time he brought it in. Then he brought it in the next year, and it received second reading, but it did not get any further than that. Then he had the experience which not many of the private members have who introduce bills in this house. The next year his bill was taken by the government of Canada and presented to this house by the government as the first Manitoba Grain Act, and placed upon the statutes of Canada. From that time till now the marketing and transportation of wheat in Canada has been largely regulated by the operations of that act as it has been amended from time to time.
We finally gave it a new name and called it the Canada Grain Act, but in all of its essential features it is the same act. So tonight I rather appreciate the opportunity of standing here at the end of fifty years' experience under that legislation to speak in favour of what the reoresentative of the constituency I now represent thought would be a good thing for the farmers of western Canada over fifty years ago.
I represent the constituency which was represented by another great farm leader of western Canada, the Hon. W. R. Motherwell. He, in 1900, organized the old territorial grain growers association. He and Dr. Douglas, who was the member that I spoke of a few moments ago, had campaigned up and down the section of western Canada which grows wheat, against the operations of the Winnipeg grain exchange, and against the operations of the railway which at that time controlled the shipment of grain to the detriment of the farm population in so far as its handling was concerned, although to their benefit in the fact that it got it away from the wheat fields to some place where it could be consumed.
But Mr. Motherwell in his day became the advocate of the formation of great co-operative organizations of farmers, which would replace the companies, if necessary, which had been handling grain in previous years, but not so much to replace them as to regulate them. And so we had set up as early as 1910 in western Canada the Co-operative Elevator Company, which was established- the first one in the province of Saskatchewan -under the leadership of the Hon. W. R. Motherwell.
Following that experience we had elevator organizations of a kind set up in the provinces on either side of us. At that time there was a Conservative government in Manitoba, and that Conservative government thought that the kind of system of elevators that they ought to have there in which to handle the grain of their province was a government-owned system, and the Roblin government established the government-owned system of elevators. They took over all the elevators in Manitoba and operated them as a government system. We in the province of Saskatchewan refused to establish a government system of elevators, but we did establish a co-operative system. May I repeat, our objective in establishing the co-operative system away back at that time was to avoid the establishment of the government system, in other words, to avoid setting up, even at that early date, of what is now known as state socialism.
The Liberal party of that day, taking that position, established in western Canada the co-operative elevator system which eventually became the pools of the present day. I wanted to give that little bit of history of the development of the systems.

We had no ceiling on wheat until 1945. The ceiling was established on September 19, 1945, at the time the five year pool was established, and as part of the set-up of the five year pool. The idea was based upon the fact that the international wheat committee was at that time discussing a five year agreement with a floor of one dollar and a ceiling of $1.50 a bushel, No. 1 northern, Fort William. When it was announced that the committee, which was meeting in London, could not agree, the Canadian government proposed a five year pool on practically the

same terms. The amount of wheat handled under this pool has been 1,435,955,510 bushels.
On July 26, 1946, the Hon. J. A. MacKinnon, then minister of trade and commerce, announced to the House of Commons the signing of the four year United Kingdom-Canadian wheat agreement. The United Kingdom-Canadian wheat agreement resulted in the sale to Britain of 631,552,419 bushels of wheat out of the total sale of 1,435,955,510. The receipts from this sale were paid into the five year pool-that is, this sale to Great Britain-and amounted to $1,089,889,013.
The operations of the pool are very simple. The farmers delivered 1,435,955,510 bushels of wheat of all grades to the wheat board. This wheat was sold in three different markets, first the home market, second the British market, and third all other markets in the world.
The amount of money received from each source was paid into the pool conducted by the wheat board. An initial payment of $1.25 a bushel, basis No. 1 northern, Fort William, was paid in 1945. Interim payments spread over the entire five years were made from time to time amounting in all to 50 cents per bushel. This makes the total payment, basis No. 1 northern, Fort William, $1.75 per bushel. The total amount paid out to date is $2,489,000,000 on 1,435,955,510 bushels.
The total amount of $2,552,333,047 was obtained from three sources: $448,649,824 was obtained from the home consumers for wheat delivered by the wheat board; $1,089,889,013 was obtained from the United Kingdom for wheat; and $1,013,810,849 was obtained from all other sources for wheat delivered by the wheat board. The Canadian government announced the other day the payment of $65 million on account of the United Kingdom into the pool. This results in there being $2,617,333,047 in the pool for distribution after costs have been deducted to producers of 1,435,955,510 bushels of wheat. The payment per bushel will amount to $1,833. When this payment is made the five year pool will be completed. I think it will be well for hon. members to keep that figure in mind because it will be used on one or two other occasions.

We will get along to that in a minute. When the five year pool was announced on September 19, 1945, the war had just ended-as a matter of fact I think

only three days earlier-and we were facing the uncertainties of the future. It was thought by most persons that prices would go down. The international wheat agreement was being advocated to stabilize prices.
Three things happened to change the situation between September 19, 1945, and June 30, 1946. Changes in the value of steel caused breaks in price controls on necessary equipment; wage increases were provided for; the Canadian loan was proposed and discussions of financial assistance to the allied countries from the United States arose. These developments made it evident that there was not likely to be any difficulty about maintaining a floor of $1 under wheat, but that the real possibility of the future was a break through the ceiling of $1.55 a bushel.
It was decided to offer the United Kingdom a four year contract-probably I should say that we started out in the beginning by offering a five year contract, but it very soon became evident that could not be considered and we offered a four year contract-with wheat delivered at $1.55 a bushel for two years, a floor under the last two years in case the unexpected happened and a price for which there was no ceiling to be arranged at least six months before the opening of the 1948 and the 1949 crop years. This contract was signed by the minister of trade and commerce, the Hon. J. A. MacKinnon, and announced by him in the House of Commons on July 26, 1946, and Mr. Strachey in the House of Commons at Westminster on July 25, 1946.

The Prime Minister re-opened the discussions while in Britain in January. After his return we were notified that the United Kingdom government preferred to consider the matter closed.
It was thought wise that because I had carried on the negotiations five years ago and when the payment for the last two years was arranged I should make an effort to have the question re-opened.
While I was in Britain I was informed-I see the press is trying to make a lot out of the fact that the matter was dealt with before I got to Britain, but it was not.

I got to Britain on Sunday. I was in touch with the government immediately. I was in touch with them again on Monday, and I was in touch with them again on Tuesday, and the announcement was not made until Tuesday afternoon.
While I was in Britain I was informed that notwithstanding the views of the Canadian government the United Kingdom government had determined that they would not make further payment, they would not make use of the $65 million remaining in the 1946 loan for the purpose and that it was their intention

Canadian Wheat Board Act
to declare that they did not intend to utilize the remaining part of the loan for any purpose. They so declared on Tuesday, February 20, while I was in London and after the matter had been discussed.
I might say in passing that those people who have such great concern for Britain and for Britain's way of doing things should accept that statement, rather than try to leave the impression that somebody tried to steal a march on somebody as this was being discussed. That did not happen. The British did discuss the question with the government here, as a matter of fact, before I left to go to Britain. I knew all about the discussion here when I left. They discussed it with me when I got over there, and they did indicate to me what they intended to do before they went into the house to do it and secured a seat for me to hear it and they discussed the matter with the whole delegation that was over from here before they went into the house to make the announcement.
This amount of money which would have been provided out of the Canadian treasury, whether loaned to the British or paid without their consent, is being utilized to make the payment amounting to 23 cents a bushel on the last two years of the agreement into the pool.
This makes a total payment under the "have regard to" clause of something between $80 million and $100 million. I think it will be agreed that the world price for 1949-50 in terms of the agreement would be not more than the ceiling price under the international wheat agreement. That was $1.80 a bushel. And the fact that there would be a ceiling price announced was dealt with in the statement of Sir Stafford Cripps in February of 1949. He on that occasion said that the world price might be lower than $2 as a result of either of two things or both, namely, that the price had gone down on the world market, or that the price was set lower under the international agreement. Well, the price set under the international agreement was $1.80 a bushel. The price actually paid by Britain for 140 million bushels of wheat was approximately $2.05 a bushel at Fort William. Had it not been for devaluation, this would have provided an adjustment of $35 million. The least it did provide was $16 million. I am prepared to agree that the settlement of 1949-50 could be held to be one of, at the outside, $35 million.
There is no doubt that was the intention of the chancellor of the exchequer in Great Britain. It was the intention of the British government; it was the intention understood by myself. I explained to the government here when I came back that the international wheat agreement price, whatever it would
be-it was then discussed as a possibility a+ $1.75; it developed to be a price of $1.80- would be interpreted as a world price under the "have regard to" clause in the wheat agreement which we had made in 1946, and since it would be considered as that, and had we not interfered in any way whatsoever with the valuation of the pound as compared with the dollar in the period in between, we would have received a settlement under that "have regard to" clause amounting to $35 million. Therefore I repeat it is not correct to say that the British have not paid anything. It is not correct to say that the British have not acknowledged the terms of the agreement, and they have done nothing at all under it. The only contention that can be put forward is the one which has been put forward by farmers and others, namely, that it is thought that they have not gone far enough. These two amounts, the amount of $65 million, which the Canadian government paid, because they did not think that the settlement was as high as it should be, and the $35 million which is accounted for by the world price in 1949, as compared with the $2.05 which we received, results in the fact that a total amount of $100 million has been paid in order to adjust the position.
I say what I am going to say now, only because it has been published in the press right across the country as having been said by Mr. Wesson himself while he was in Britain that the representation made there was that the British could settle what the farmers considered to be their obligation by paying, or arranging for the payment of, $100 million. I am sure if everyone were satisfied that $100 million has been provided under the terms of the agreement there would be general satisfaction among the farmers of western Canada. All that was necessary to put us all behind such a settlement was the consent of the British government. There never was any question in our mind that this amount of money ought to be paid, and all this talk about disagreement and discussions that have taken place in the government is just so much eyewash. The discussions lasted about half an hour, and took place just a few days ago.

This means that the wheat delivered +o the United Kingdom earned for the producer an average of $1 -828 a bushel at Fort William. The payments made to the farmers when completed will amount to an average of $1.82 a bushel, from the five year pool. Now, I would ask members of this house this question: How much more equitable can a price be made? The British contract, as it has been settled with the payment of $65 million, brings $1.82 into the pool. The sale of wheat to Canadians, and all other people outside the British contract, brought $1.82 a bushel into the pool; and when we are paying it out we are paying on the basis of $1-833 for No. 1 northern. The payments made to
farmers when completed will amount to $1.82 a bushel. This is two cents above the figure which has been written into the international wheat agreement as satisfactory to farmers. And who settled that figure? That figure was settled by the farm representatives from all the exporting countries in the world, meeting with the importers from all the importing countries in the world. And every leader of the farm movement in the Dominion of Canada was present at the time, and they declared that a reasonable ceiling price for

wheat in Canada, not in the past five years, but in the years ahead, was $1.80 a bushel.
This contract, this pool, brought the farmers for the last five years two cents a bushel more than that. What criticism could there be made of it? As a matter of fact there is nothing in connection with that to criticize.
Some parties continue to contend that if wheat had been sold on the open market the farmer would have obtained $330 million more for the wheat sold under the four year United Kingdom-Canadian wheat agreement.
In the first place there has been no open market for Canadian wheat anywhere in the world, outside Great Britain, since 1941. The reason for that is obvious. We were at war during the greater part of that time. I hope the Winnipeg Free Press will not say that I am saying there has been no world market. I have made the statement that I am making now on a number of other occasions, and everyone who has quoted it has said that I have said there was no world market. I have said there was no open market. And there has been no open market.
There has been an embargo against our wheat going into the United States for human consumption since 1941. We are not permitted to ship it there. Before that there was a prohibitive duty of 42 cents a bushel. Since the Marshall plan was set up, if we had been pouring our wheat into European countries and thus using up American dollars, wheat could at any time have been declared surplus. Even though wheat was not declared surplus one country after another which usually obtained its wheat from Canada, but was receiving Marshall aid, considered it wise to take their wheat from the United States. The result of that was that Canada dropped from a position where she supplied 40 per cent of the wheat which entered into international trade to a position where she supplied only 22 per cent of the wheat which entered into international trade. This position would have been much worse, had there been no United Kingdom-Canadian agreement.
In the second place, the class II wheat price which is used as the basis for figuring the loss up to $330 million is the price which the United States government paid American dealers for wheat-much of which they were trading to get their dollars back, and much of which they were giving away-plus the increased value of Canadian wheat because of greater protein content.
There was less than 72 million bushels of this class II wheat sold in 1946-47 and less than 17 million bushels in 1947-48, or less than 89 million bushels peddled over the

world, while 340 million bushels, or lour times as much, was being sold to Great Britain alone. If we had left the British market to Marshall aid and attempted to peddle 430 million bushels of wheat over the world under after-the-war conditions, we would have had to give much of it away or lend the dollars to countries which could never pay it back to get rid of our wheat. The argument is a ridiculous attempt to mislead farmers, and it is used only for that purpose, Mr. Speaker. No such loss would have been experienced if Britain had paid nothing under the "have regard to" clause, or if the Canadian government had not paid the $65 million. It is just possible that the Canadian farmer received more because of the four year contract than he could have received under any other system.
The fact is that the western farmers accepted the wheat board as the agency to sell their wheat. They accepted it as a result of those agitations which I stated at the beginning began back around 1900. They sold 636 million bushels to be delivered over four years to the United Kingdom government. The government of Canada is behind the financing of the wheat board and considers that the farmers were entitled under that agreement to $65 million more than they were paid.
The whole experience is conclusive proof that the farmers were well advised when they asked to have their wheat marketed under the terms of the wheat board act, now before parliament for amendment.
The act may require further amendment from time to time; but in my opinion the farmers of the west have not been convinced that they have lost money under the system of wheat board marketing as compared with any other system. Any hon. member of this house who thinks that he is going to be able to break the impression which western farmers have of the system under which they have been marketing their grains over a period of years by suggesting that there is any other system that ever brought home returns similar to those ought to recall that in no other five year period, either in wartime or in peacetime, did the farmer ever get so much for his wheat as he got for his wheat over the last five years.
One of the brightest young farmers in western Canada said to me the other day, "If the government will guarantee that I will get as much for my wheat on the average over the next five years as I got under this system for the last years, I will sell all my wheat now."

On June 5, 1950, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), having made no statement with regard to the five year pool, was questioned in the house about it to see if we could not get some information as to whether a settlement had been reached concerning the "have regard to" clause when he was in Great Britain in the latter part of May. On questioning he made it quite definite. There is no doubt about the minister's words. At page 3221 of Hansard for June 5, 1950, he stated:
The "have regard to" clause reads as follows:
"The actual price to be paid for wheat to be bought and sold within the crop year 1948-49 shall be negotiated and settled between the United Kingdom and the government of Canada not later than the 31st December, 1947, and prices for wheat to be bought and sold within the crop year 1949-50 shall be negotiated and settled not later than the 31st December, 1948. In determining the prices of these two crop years, 1948-49 and 1949-50, the United Kingdom government will have regard to any difference between the prices paid under this agreement in the 1946-47 and 1947-48 crop years and the world prices for wheat in 1946-47 and 1947-48 crop years."
The minister goes on to say:
That is the "have regard to" clause in the agreement. I suggest that regard was paid in fixing these prices.
That is the Minister of Trade and Commerce speaking in the house. He continues:
The price for the first two years of the agreement was $1.55. After negotiation the price for the third year was fixed at $2, and after negotiation the price for the fourth year was fixed at $2. What does my hon, friend read out of the agreement beyond the fact that the price for the last two years would be settled having regard to world prices in the first two years?
Later on he continues as follows:
The matter of the "have regard to" clause was discussed in great detail during our sessions with Sir Stafford Cripps and other ministers of the United Kingdom government. The whole situation was reviewed. The United Kingdom is just as positive as I have been in my statements in the house as to what the world price of wheat really was in those periods. My hon. friend said the world price was the price in a local market to which Canadian grain is not permitted access. I wonder what the world price would have been if we had been able to ship our Canadian grain to the Chicago market, which he says is the great criterion for world prices. We went over the agreement while in London. We asked the United Kingdom government what further settlement it is to make on account of the "have regard to" clause. The United Kingdom government took a very strong position that they had fulfilled all obligations under that clause, and so far as the United Kingdom was concerned. We agreed on behalf of Canada that considering all the circumstances that was the case.
That is pretty positive. I am sending to the Minister of Trade and Commerce the statement that appeared in the government publication. It is quite clear from what I

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, I am entitled to keep the record straight so far as I am concerned. I may say that the discussions about the disposal of the 1950 crop took place before there was any mention of the five year pool. That matter was discussed and settled and then discussions were opened on the five year pool, against our wishes really. I made it clear at the outset I had no authority to discuss or settle. I told those present that we looked to the minister who negotiated the agreement in the first place to negotiate the settlement, and that all I could do was carry back a report of the discussions. Nevertheless when the discussions continued I got a very positive statement from the chancellor of the exchequer, and there were other ministers present. I had to take their views back to my colleagues as the position of the United Kingdom government. I reported that position to them. The decision, if there was any decision, was made after I returned.

Those were the statements made in this house by the Minister of Trade and Commerce who is in charge of this

Canadian Wheat Board Act
department, according to revised Hansard; and I think we as members are entitled to quote them. I believe members of the house and the people of Canada are entitled to believe what they read in revised Hansard, and not have ministers come back six months later and begin to revise it again under circumstances which make it pretty obvious that they are not satisfied with what they said before.
The other point I want to deal with in respect to this agreement is whether the farmers in western Canada are entitled to more than 8-3 cents per bushel. We hear a great deal of comment around this building that the western farmers are asking for a subsidy; that this $65 million is just a handout to the west. We see articles in the press saying that the west has again gouged the government of Canada out of a further $65 million. I want to point out some of the reasons why we in western Canada believe we are entitled to this money.
What were the conditions at the time the British agreement was entered into? You will remember that was back in 1945 and the early part of 1946, just at the time price controls were being removed in Canada. There was a discussion in this house as to whether or not the British agreement was satisfactory; certain questions were asked and certain statements were made in this house in reply. The Minister of Agriculture himself made certain statements, and the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar asked certain questions with respect to what would happen if the cost of the things the farmer had to use in the production of his crop were to increase. Let me quote from page 4825 of Hansard for August 15, 1946. At that time the house was discussing the floor price legislation and this agreement.
If what the minister says is correct and parity over the period of the agreement should be in the neighbourhood of $1.40 or $1.35, or whatever it may be, of course that would be a different story, but the point I think I made quite clearly was that if costs of production and costs of living continue to rise, a compensatory adjustment should be made out of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada.
That was the statement of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, and later on the Minister of Agriculture had this to say:
We shall not insist on the matter of time, and anyway we are in committee. What I want to point out is that under the floor price measure-and that is not the proper name, but it will do-we stated to the house that $200 million was being provided for the purpose of taking care of any adjustments in connection with what might be known as parity on other farm products. At the same time we stated to the house that similar arrangements would be made if necessary, through the wheat board, in connection with grain. I just want to point out that provision is made in another way.
In other words the minister gave this house the assurance that should the cost of production of wheat continue to rise, some compensatory adjustment would be made by this government-not by the British government but this government-to take care of that increased cost. What has taken place in the meantime? According to Professor McDougall of Queen's university, taking the purchasing value of the wheat dollar from 1935 to 1939 as $1, from 1904 to 1914 the value of that dollar in terms of wheat was $1.28. In 1947-48 it was 97 cents; in 1949-50 it was 80 cents. Today it is only 71 cents. In other words the cost of the things the farmer has to buy to produce his crop has increased by over 30 per cent. Therefore the farmer is entitled to some compensation for that increased cost of production which this government allowed to take place. Not only that, but look at the cost of living index. It has jumped from approximately 121 in 1946 to 175-2 today, which means that the value of the 8-3 cents payment we are getting is about 5 cents as compared to the purchasing power in 1946.
These are facts you cannot get away from. It is not a case of the western farmer trying to get something to which he is not entitled. Through all their organizations the western producers have stated that they believe they are entitled to from 15 to 25 cents by way of final payment, and we in this group believe that also. We believe that because of the policies this government followed in reducing the value of the Canadian dollar by allowing inflation in this country, in view of the policies which it followed, and which have caused increases in the cost of production, the government owes the western farmer a reasonable payment on this five year pool. They have failed to get a further settlement from the British government, but that does not remove their responsibility to the farmers in western Canada. I am therefore going to move, seconded by the member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce), a subamendment to the amendment moved by the member for Souris (Mr. Ross), as follows:
That the amendment be amended by deleting therefrom all the words after the words "final settlement of the five-year wheat pool," and substituting therefor the following words:	It being the opinion
of this house that consideration should be given to a final payment of twenty-five cents per bushel.
